opus-5.5.text:
I think the core reason is that model development itself is a very long-horizon, multi-step task. If you look at what a researcher actually does, it's not answering one question. You form a hypothesis, write code, design an experiment, launch training, watch the curves, find that something went wrong, debug it, read papers, compare results, and then decide what to try next. Each of those steps involves interacting with an environment: a codebase, a cluster, a dataset, evaluation results. That is exactly what we mean by agentic capability.

A model that can only produce a good single answer is like a very smart person who can only speak one sentence and then has to stop. They might have great intuition, but they can't carry an idea through to verification. Innovation requires closing the loop: proposing something, testing it against reality, getting feedback, and iterating. Without the ability to take actions, use tools, and keep a coherent goal over hundreds or thousands of steps, the model can't close that loop by itself.

There's another angle. Pretraining data is finite, and the high-quality human data is being used up. So the next source of progress has to come from the model generating its own experience by interacting with environments and learning from the outcomes. Agentic capability is what makes that possible. Once a model can work productively in environments, you can scale the amount of feedback it gets, and that becomes a new scaling dimension.

So if you ask whether models can eventually help develop better models, I'd say the prerequisite is not just being smarter on benchmarks. It's being able to do the actual work of research end to end: reliably, over long horizons, with good judgment about what to try next. That's why I see agentic ability as the foundation. Intelligence that can't act can't really innovate; it can only suggest. Once the model can act and verify, it starts to become a participant in the research process itself, and that's when things could accelerate.

r001.rationale: The candidate says models may help develop better models and become participants in the research process, framing this as a route to accelerated innovation.

r002.rationale: The candidate explains that models can test ideas, observe experimental feedback, debug failures, and decide what to try next.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the simplest way to put it is that model development itself is a kind of agentic task. If you look at what a researcher actually does all day, it's not writing one elegant equation. It's running experiments, reading the logs, forming a hypothesis about why something didn't work, changing the data mix or the hyperparameters, launching again, and iterating over weeks. It's a long-horizon loop of acting, observing, and adjusting. That's exactly the shape of what we call agentic capability.

So if a model can only answer questions in a single turn, it can help you brainstorm, but it can't really participate in that loop. It can't own a problem. The moment a model can plan over many steps, use tools, run code, look at the results and recover from mistakes, it starts to look like a junior researcher instead of a search engine. And that's when it can begin contributing to its own development, whether that's writing training infrastructure, proposing data pipelines, or debugging a run that diverged at 3am.

The reason I think this matters so much is that the bottleneck in this field is increasingly human iteration speed, not compute alone. Everyone has GPUs. What's scarce is the number of good experiments you can run and learn from per week. If the model itself can take over a large share of that experimental loop, then progress compounds. The model gets better, so it becomes a better research assistant, so the next model gets better faster. Agentic capability is the thing that closes that loop.

There's also a scientific point. Reasoning that happens entirely inside the model's head has a ceiling, because the model can't check itself against reality. An agent that can execute code and see what actually happens gets feedback from the world, not just from its own prior. That grounding is what turns a plausible idea into a verified one, and verification is the core of research. So I don't see agents as a product feature layered on top of the model. I see them as the mechanism by which models eventually become real participants in the science of building models.

r001.rationale: The response describes models contributing to their own development and says this feedback loop helps build the next model faster.

r002.rationale: It explains that agents can run experiments, inspect results, revise hypotheses or settings, and iterate.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is that model development is a process, not a single question with a single answer. You have an idea, implement it, run an experiment, look at the results, and decide what to try next. If a model can only suggest an architecture or write a piece of code, a human still has to drive that whole loop.

Agentic capability allows the model to participate in that loop much more independently. It needs to use tools, track experiments, debug failures, and adjust its approach based on evidence. That is what makes it possible to move from proposing ideas to actually testing them.

But I would call it a foundation rather than a sufficient condition. You also need good research judgment and the ability to generate useful hypotheses. An agent can execute a lot of experiments without discovering anything important. The opportunity is to combine those capabilities: generate an idea, test it rigorously, learn from the result, and keep going. That’s the kind of process through which models could contribute to innovation in model development.

r001.rationale: The response discusses models contributing to innovation in model development, but does not identify developing their successors as the key locus.

r002.rationale: It says models can adjust their approach based on evidence and learn from experiment results, then continue testing.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is that model development is an iterative process. It’s not enough for a model to suggest an interesting architecture or a new training method. It has to implement the idea, run experiments, look at the results, identify what went wrong, and decide what to try next. That whole loop requires agentic capability.

And research is particularly challenging because you don’t know the correct answer in advance. An experiment can fail, or it can produce a result that looks promising but doesn’t actually support your hypothesis. The model needs to maintain a goal over many steps, use tools, and update its judgment based on evidence.

So I see agentic capability as a foundation, although it isn’t sufficient by itself. You also need strong reasoning and the ability to generate useful hypotheses. But agency is what allows those ideas to be tested and refined. Without that, the model can help you discuss research; with it, the model can start to carry out research.

r001.rationale: The response says models with agency can carry out and refine research, but it does not identify models developing their successors as a key locus of AI innovation.

r002.rationale: It explains that models can use experimental results to identify problems and decide what to try next, revising and refining research ideas based on evidence.
